answer.exemplar: With four supporting strands the load is shared between them, so in the ideal case each strand carries one quarter of the load and the effort must be the load divided by four. questions.stem: Slower this season, the extractor drum lost speed as the honey built up on the walls. I wrote down why in the log.

answer.exemplar: When the spinning honey sticks to the inside of the drum, the mass of the system increases and its moment of inertia grows by the amount of that mass times the square of the radius. The kinetic energy that has been lost is dissipated as heat in the honey and the drum walls.

questions.explanation: A good answer says the added mass raises the moment of inertia and, with angular momentum conserved, the drum slows. A poor answer claims the honey drags on the walls or that momentum is lost.

answer.exemplar: A torque does not by itself specify how fast work is being done, so the power delivered is the product of the torque and the angular speed of the shaft. questions.stem: Describing the block and tackle in the barn, I explained in the log how the four strands change the effort needed to raise the load.

answer.exemplar: A block and tackle does not reduce the work that has to be done; it only spreads the load over several supporting strands of rope. questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: A mass dropped onto a spinning wheel and stuck to it
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a motor must respond as a drum loads up with honey
questions.stem: The extractor drum lost speed as the honey built up on the walls, and I wrote in the log how the motor has to respond to hold the set speed.

answer.exemplar: As the honey sticks to the wall of the drum, the moment of inertia of the drum and its load rises, so for the same motor torque the angular speed would fall. To hold the set speed the motor must supply a larger torque, because the torque required to keep a body turning at a fixed speed is the rate of change of angular momentum, and the angular momentum needed grows with the inertia. In practice the drum is run at a set speed and the motor supplies whatever torque that demands.

questions.explanation: A good answer says the inertia rises so more torque is needed to hold the speed, and links this to the growth of angular momentum. A poor answer says the motor torque never changes with the load.
questions.hint: More inertia at the same speed needs more torque.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Acceleration of a falling spool as its cord unwinds
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the cord tension on a falling spool
questions.stem: Working the spool numbers: a cylindrical spool of mass 0.60 kg and radius 0.10 m unwinds from a fixed cord. With g 9.8 m per s squared, what is the tension in the cord as it descends?
questions.explanation: For a solid cylinder the acceleration is two thirds of g, which is 6.53 m per s squared, so the tension is m times g minus a, giving 1.96 N. Using the full weight would ignore the force that spins the spool.
questions.hint: Tension is the weight minus the accelerating force.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why a falling spool falls more slowly than a falling weight
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the fall time of a hoop spool
questions.stem: The fall time of the hoop spool from the shed roof was recorded as slower than for the solid cylinder. With a hoop acceleration of 4.9 m per s squared, how long does it take to fall 5.0 m from rest?
questions.explanation: From rest the distance is half a t squared, so t is the root of 10.0 over 4.9 giving 1.43 s. The solid cylinder, accelerating at 6.54 m per s squared, would take only 1.24 s.
questions.hint: Use s equals half a t squared from rest.
